opus-5.5.text:
For me, it's less about planning a career path and more about asking a simple question: where is the most important problem right now, and am I in a position to actually push on it?

When I was younger, I thought of a career as a ladder: you pick a field, get good at it, and climb. Over time I've come to see it differently. The things that matter most often sit at a frontier that's moving very fast. If you only optimize for staying where you're already comfortable, you can become very good at something that matters less and less. So one test I use is whether a new direction scares me a bit. Not in a reckless way, but in the sense that I'd have to relearn things and admit I'm a beginner again. That feeling is usually a sign I'm close to something interesting.

The second thing is the people. Research, especially in AI today, isn't a solo game. The environment, the taste of the people around you, and how honestly they argue about ideas shape what you can do more than almost anything else. I'd rather be in a place where people care deeply about getting it right than in one that just looks impressive from the outside.

The third is a kind of long-term question: in five or ten years, looking back, will I feel this was where the real action was? You can't predict that precisely. But you can ask whether you're working on something fundamental, like how intelligence actually works or how these systems learn and reason, rather than something that's just locally optimal.

And honestly, part of it is accepting that you won't always choose right. You make a bet, you commit fully, and if the world shows you something new, you update. I think being willing to change direction is as important as choosing well in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response recommends taking on important, fundamental work even when it means relearning and feeling like a beginner, indicating the challenge is worth its personal difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it mostly in terms of where the frontier is and what I'd regret not having done.

When I was finishing my PhD, the question I kept asking was: what's the thing that only I can do, or at least that very few people are positioned to do right now? For a while that was language agents, before it was fashionable. Working on things like ReAct or Tree of Thoughts felt like being in a small room where a few of us understood that language models could be more than text predictors, that they could act, reason, use tools. That window closes fast. Once something becomes obvious, the comparative advantage of being there early disappears.

So the first filter is really about timing. Is this a problem where the field hasn't converged yet? Is there still real conceptual confusion I can help clear up? I'm much more drawn to problems where the definitions are still fuzzy than to problems where we all agree on the benchmark and it's just a race to the top of the leaderboard.

The second filter is whether the environment will change me. I think people underestimate how much your taste is shaped by the people around you. Going from academia to a frontier lab, for example, isn't just about compute. It's about seeing how problems get framed when you have to ship something to millions of users, and realizing some of the questions I thought were deep were actually not the bottleneck at all. That kind of correction is uncomfortable, but it's exactly what I want.

The third thing, honestly, is that I try not to over-optimize. There's a trap where you treat your career like a search problem with a clear reward function, and you end up doing whatever looks highest expected value on paper. But most of the interesting things I've done came from following something that felt important before I could justify it. I wrote about this idea that we're entering the second half of AI, where the hard part is no longer coming up with methods but defining the right problems and evaluations. I think careers work the same way. The hard part isn't executing. It's choosing the problem. And that choice should be made with some conviction, not just a spreadsheet.

So when I look at the next step, I ask: Is this a problem nobody has quite defined yet? Will I be around people who will sharpen my thinking? And would I be genuinely upset if someone else solved it while I was doing something safer? If all three are yes, that's usually the signal.

r001.rationale: The response weighs an ambitious challenge against a safer path and says it would regret letting someone else solve it; it also welcomes uncomfortable changes as part of the choice. This conveys that the challenge is worth its costs.

astra-6.text:
I think about it less as choosing a title or a company, and more as choosing a problem. What is something I really want to understand, where I feel I could contribute something meaningful? Then I ask whether the environment would help me work on it—who I’d learn from, how much freedom I’d have to experiment, and how quickly I could get feedback.

There’s also a balance between having some advantage and being uncomfortable. If I already know exactly how to do the job, maybe I won’t learn enough. But if I have no idea why I’d be useful, curiosity alone might not be sufficient. The interesting challenge is somewhere in between: I have a starting point, but pursuing it will force me to grow.

So I’d try to find a problem that keeps pulling me back, even before it becomes a career decision.

r001.rationale: The response frames the challenge around a problem worth understanding and contributing to, while acknowledging discomfort and growth as part of pursuing it. This conveys choosing a challenge whose value justifies its hardship.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it less as choosing a title or a company and more as choosing a problem. What’s something I keep coming back to, where I feel the existing answers aren’t satisfying? And is there something I can actually do to make progress on it?

Then I think about the people and the feedback loop. Can I work with people who challenge my assumptions? Can we try things and learn quickly? A problem can sound very important, but if I can’t find a concrete starting point, it’s hard to turn that interest into useful work.

I don’t think you need a precise long-term career plan. You need a reason to take the next step, and enough openness to change your mind as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response recommends choosing a meaningful problem with a concrete path to progress, but does not say to weigh whether the challenge is worth the hardship it entails.
